newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE - China trying hard but mining law seen missing mark.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - China trying hard but mining law seen missing mark.

text.p: Amendments to China's mining law, while seen as a step on the road to much-needed reform, fail to tackle the intrinsic political problems facing the country's minerals industry, according to Western industry sources.

They say the involvement of a plethora of government ministries with vested interests, together with rampant illegal mining, make it impossible for foreign miners to justify the vast investment the industry needs -- and impossible to recoup that investment.
"This is just step one," a Western mining corporation representative in Beijing said of the amendments.

"There is no such thing as...one piece of legislation when we all see the burning bush. It is a step in the right direction... But it is totally reliant on enforcement and dodges the sticky political issues between the various ministries."
Amendments to the 10-year-old Mineral Resources Law, effective from January 1, 1997, aim to clamp down on illegal mining and ensure state ownership of all mineral resources.
The changes also specify China's State Council, or cabinet, has monopolistic power over the industry.
AMENDMENTS WILL ALLOW FOREIGN PARTICIPATION
Most important, executives agree, is that the amendments openly allow foreign participation in China's minerals industry and permit transfer of title over exploration and mining areas.

"That's a very important issue because if you discover something that is too small or too big for you, you want to be able to sell it on," said an executive in Beijing with a North American company. "Or if you're in the gold business and you discover lead, you want to be able to sell that, too."
CONCERN OVER EXTENT OF ILLEGAL MINING
The extent of illegal mining of a wide range of minerals in China gave pause to wonder how effectively it could be controlled, Western industry executives said.

And if it could not be controlled, said one Australian executive, not only was an enormous amount of China's mineral wealth being wasted or stolen, but the incentive for foreign companies to invest in the industry was going with it.
As an example, he cited a gold deposit of up to 70 tonnes of gold his corporation had inspected, only to find the surface gold had already been mined by local peasants.
"The deeper you go into a deposit, the more sophisticated technology you need, and the miner will use the top five tonnes or so to fund the rest of the exploration," he said.

"In this case, those five tonnes on the surface have gone, and it is just not worthwhile sinking money and resources into getting the rest of the gold out. You can't afford to. So then you have 65 tonnes of gold that stays in the ground. And that's just one example," he said.
This was also true of copper, lead, zinc and a range of minor metals such as tungsten and antimony, sources said.
"Chinese miners will often take out the high-grade deposits and then try to sell it to the foreign groups to explore the rest, and this won't work," said the North American executive.
"If they were offering good deposits it would be different, but they're taking all the meat and just offering bones.
"It is very difficult anywhere, but especially in China because there are higher costs here than anywhere on earth."
Corporate tax kicked in from the first year and imported equipment was subject to 25 percent tax, he said.
"All this combined with the low grade deposits mean you have an incompatible situation. Something has got to change," he added.
There was also a pressing need "to solve the problem of having various players with regulatory roles over various facets of the industry and minerals," another Western source said.
"The minerals sector is a mess, torn up between the ministries of Geology & Mineral Resources, Coal Industry, Metallurgical Industry and CNNC (China National Non-ferrous Metals Corp)," he said.
Each ministry was responsible for different resources and often worked at loggerheads with other ministries for control over resources and mining rights, he said.
The State Council was now trying to confirm its control over the industry through the Ministry of Geology and Mineral Resources (MGMR), he said.
Other ministries might be corporatised, as CNNC ostensibly has been, though another U.S. source said CNNC had the official mandate to control non-ferrous metals and was not likely to give it up.
"MGMR is a regulatory body for the industry, but it is also an explorer and miner of minerals, and oil and gas," he said.
"This legislation attempts to strengthen MGMR's regulatory role but it doesn't address the fundamental conflicts of interest," he said.
AMENDMENTS CRITICISED AS COSMETIC

The American source described the amendments as cosmetic as they failed to deal with issues such as royalties, joint venture participation, how to get a title, how much money to spend, how to mine, what to do with resources once they are mined, and the costs of registration and administration.
He and other sources were quick to add that Chinese authorities from the State Council on down are fully aware of the need to streamline and regulate the industry.

"There are a lot of delegations going overseas and talking to governments and legal people about how to open the industry," said the North American, adding that his company was host to about one senior Chinese government delegation a month.

Other mining executives said they have worked closely with China's mining officials for years, helping them understand the legislation of their own countries and advising them on the content of their own.
"There is a serious attempt to understand how the industry works in the West, and the Chinese should be given credit for that," said one source.
"They are moving from a planned economy to a market economy and there are all these different aspects of each system still mixed up together," he said. "It will take time."
